data.title: Svätý Jur – Neštich, a hillfort with two thousand years of occupation
data.excerpt: The Neštich hillfort is the oldest surviving trace of building on the territory of the town of Svätý Jur, and evidence of continuous occupation of the area over two millennia. Whole generations of local people fled here in times of danger, and even today its defensive system and its vast area are astonishing.
data.metaTitle: Svätý Jur – Neštich: a hillfort of two millennia
data.metaDescription: Neštich, the oldest surviving building remains at Svätý Jur: a massive defensive system and a vast refuge used by the people of two millennia.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Part of the Bratislava Gate, one of four hillforts guarding the south-eastern frontier of Great Moravia (together with Bratislava, Devín and Devínska Nová Ves)

keyFacts.label: Area
keyFacts.value: 3.26 ha in total (Enclosures IV and III and Baileys I and II); after the baileys were added, the fortified area reached a length of about 680 m

keyFacts.label: Construction of the acropolis wall
keyFacts.value: Earth with stones reinforced by timber beams (grillages); wall on the bailey side at least 4.5 m wide, conical ditch (2.6 m wide, 1.5 m deep)

keyFacts.label: Finds of the upper stratum
keyFacts.value: Bronze earrings (paralleled at the Lupka cemetery in Nitra), stirrups, a splendid riding stirrup, a hoard of seven earrings in Byzantine-Oriental style

keyFacts.label: Crafts
keyFacts.value: Iron production attested, smith's tongs, axe-shaped currency bars as currency, wheel-thrown pottery — but no craft workshops

keyFacts.label: Medieval water pipeline
keyFacts.value: Clay pipeline several kilometres long, individual sections 55–58 cm long, with small shafts for venting

keyFacts.label: Excavation
keyFacts.value: Detailed archaeological excavation led by PhDr. Július Vavák; results published in Zo starších dejín Svätého Jura (2010)

timeline.description: A bronze openwork mount depicting a griffin (an Avar bronze also popular among the Slavs), found on the first bailey.

timeline.title: The first fortification is built
timeline.description: The presumed earlier unfortified settlement was partly enclosed by ramparts on the acropolis; the fortification became a refuge for the adjoining open hamlet.

timeline.title: The hillfort arises as a defensive element
timeline.description: The most probable time of its origin, connected with the fighting between the Moravian and the Nitra principalities — the hillfort as a defensive element of the northern frontier of the Nitra region.

timeline.year: before the rise of Great Moravia
timeline.title: A centre of regional administration
timeline.description: The hillfort became a centre of regional administration controlled by an emerging power elite — at this time and in this area without parallel apart from Devín.

timeline.title: Great Moravia arises — the hillfort flourishes
timeline.description: The union of the two lands was followed by the extension of the fortification by the first bailey.

timeline.year: the second half of the 9th century
timeline.title: The second bailey is built
timeline.description: The hillfort experiences a further flowering as a regional centre and a centre of crafts; the total length of the fortified area reached approximately 680 m.

timeline.year: late 9th – first half of the 10th century
timeline.title: The hut with the jewellery hoard on the acropolis burns down
timeline.description: The dwelling with its hoard of seven earrings, a gombík, a finger ring, a vessel, a spearhead and a dagger was destroyed by fire.

timeline.description: Finds at the hillfort are temporarily interrupted; for the next 200 years or so the hillfort served only as a temporary refuge during attacks.

timeline.title: Renewal by the counts of Svätý Jur and Pezinok
timeline.description: Permanent occupation renewed; a palace building, a water cistern and a clay pipeline about 3 km long were built; the rampart system was renewed with a new gateway.

timeline.title: The move to Biely Kameň castle
timeline.description: The counts set about building a stone castle on the hill on the other side of the valley; a permanent garrison was still maintained at Neštich for a considerable time.

timeline.title: The hillfort finally abandoned
timeline.description: After it was abandoned there was never again permanent occupation, although the rampart system may have served as a refuge in later fighting too.

children.text: The Neštich hillfort represents the oldest surviving remains of building on the territory of the town of Svätý Jur. It is also evidence of the continuous occupation of this area over the course of two millennia and a place to which whole generations of local inhabitants fled in times of danger. Even though, some 700 years after it was abandoned, we can see only the remnants of its former glory, its defensive system and its enormous area can still astonish us.

Hillforts played an irreplaceable role in the history of Great Moravia. Besides their defensive function they also served as political and administrative centres, seats of the upper social stratum, stores of goods and places suited to the development of craft production.
On the south-eastern section of the Great Moravian frontier, also called the Bratislava Gate, these tasks were performed by four hillforts – at Bratislava, Devín, Devínska Nová Ves and Neštich.
Pre-Slavic occupation at the Hradisko site

From what is known about the cultures living in the territory of present-day Slovakia, we know that the building of hillforts was typical of the Slavs. With its outstanding position, however, the hill on which the hillfort stands today also attracted the attention of the peoples who inhabited this area before the Slavs.

Perhaps the oldest of these peoples were the Germanic peoples, who lived in this territory shortly after the turn of the era and created here a political entity known as the Kingdom of Vannius. Finds of Germanic iron axes date from their time. One of the most recent finds also belongs here – a silver denarius of Antoninus Pius, struck between 138 and 161. Since we know only a small number of finds from this period, it is highly probable that the area of the hillfort was used only as a refuge – a temporary settlement used only in times of danger.
The Slavs at the Hradisko

The most probable time of the hillfort's origin is the 830s. It was precisely then that the fighting between the Moravian and the Nitra principalities began, and it was precisely then that the hillfort may have come into being as a defensive element of the northern frontier of the Principality of Nitra.

The oldest part of the hillfort is probably the oval enclosure on the highest part of the hill, designated Enclosure IV. After it came into being, a permanent garrison was stationed here. After one of the attacks, Enclosure III was gradually built as well, and with the constantly growing tension of the following decades also Baileys I and II. The whole complex thus came to cover 3.26 ha, of which about half belongs to the hillfort proper. The building of such an extensive structure is evidence of the existence of an organised society, but also of dense occupation of the area, because large numbers of people must have worked on the construction over the long years of building.

children.text: In accordance with the customs of the time, the hillfort complex was arranged so that persons of distinction and soldiers resided in the highest (and at the same time oldest) part. Wealthy women must have lived here too, as the finds of bronze earrings show. Similar earrings are known only from the hillfort at Nitra (the Lupka cemetery), which testifies to a connection that existed between the two sites. Equally important are the finds of a stirrup, of earrings with a double pendant and also of two vessels preserved whole.

The ordinary inhabitants were settled in the second part of the hillfort (Enclosure III). Farm buildings must have stood here as well. Iron production is attested, but not its working. The remains of not a single craft workshop have been found.

Judging from the finds at other hillforts it is highly probable that a sacral building must also have stood at the hillfort. Because of the enormous area, however, its early discovery is unlikely. Nor is it certain that it was made of durable material whose remains could have survived to the present day.

children.text: Neštich is one of the few Slavic hillforts where a detailed archaeological excavation is currently under way, led by PhDr. Július Vavák. The current results of the excavations were published in „Zo starších dejín Svätého Jura“ (From the Earlier History of Svätý Jur) 2010, a collective monograph (which, together with other books, can be bought at the Little Carpathian Museum in Pezinok). The insights that follow are drawn mainly from this publication.
Finds – the period of the Avar Khaganate

Among the oldest objects with which the presence of the Slavs can be associated is a fragment of an iron Slavic spur with a hook. Particularly important are the finds of so-called Avar bronzes from the Hradisko site, which also found favour among the Slavs. One is a bronze openwork mount depicting a griffin, found on the first bailey, close to the bailey rampart and the acropolis rampart. The object is so far the oldest find that can be linked to the presence of the Slavs at the hillfort. It belongs to phase I of the Late Avar period (between 720 and 750). Later Avar mounts are also known from the site.

children.text: Further interesting finds are artefacts of western origin, or their derivatives, which can be dated to the period of the so-called Blatnica–Mikulčice horizon, and their occurrence partly overlaps with the circulation of the Avar bronzes. A stirrup inlaid with bronze found in the bailey rampart, iron tongue-shaped strap ends from belts, a segmented belt loop, a small plate decorated with chip carving. The Late Avar mounts, as well as other objects from the surroundings of the hillfort, clearly point to an interest in the site attested at the latest by about the middle of the 8th century. The presumed, indirectly attested earlier unfortified settlement may soon afterwards have been partly enclosed by ramparts on the least accessible part – the acropolis – at the latest in the last decades of the 8th century. The fortification became a refuge for the inhabitants of the adjoining open hamlet. Evidence of the destruction horizon of this open settlement consists of burnt pottery, daub, animal bones, a Carolingian stirrup found in the bailey rampart, and finally the distribution of the Avar bronzes. The archaeological excavation and the finds from private collections of recent years clearly confirm V. Turčan's assumption that before the rise of Great Moravia the hillfort became a centre of regional administration, controlled by an emerging power elite that commanded military force. The character of the finds from the hillfort even points to the fact that this was an important centre with no parallel at this time and in this area apart from the hillfort at Devín. After the rise of Great Moravia in 833 we can follow a further flowering of the Svätý Jur hillfort as a regional centre and a centre of crafts. We see it in the extension of the fortification by a bailey, which most probably took place after the union of the two lands. In the second half of the 9th century the hillfort experiences a flowering which, besides the building of the first bailey, was expressed in the building of a second bailey. The continuing existence of the hillfort testifies to its importance even after the union of the lands, when the Nitra region evidently retained a certain degree of independence, which was expressed also in the conflicts between the princes of Nitra and those of Moravia.
Weapons – evidence of the presence of a ruling stratum

Evidence of a military component among the settlers is provided by finds of weapons, axes, numerous arrowheads and spearheads/javelins. Two axes have been known from the Hradisko site so far, one slender form and part of a bearded axe. A further seven axes from this find spot, however, are in private collections. Among the more recent finds it is above all the spears/javelins that deserve attention. Of the militaria, arrowheads are the most numerous, especially barbed ones, with fewer leaf-shaped and three-bladed forms. The splendid stirrup mentioned above belonged to a rider's equipment and certainly belonged to a member of the upper social stratum. Among the more recent finds let us pause over the spurs and the cheek-pieces of horse bits. Belt buckles represent more common finds. An important part of a warrior's equipment were also the costly mail shirts, rings from which we have found at several places in the hillfort.
Tools

Numerous pieces of evidence of the life of its inhabitants have also been found at the hillfort, represented by objects of personal use such as pottery vessels and their fragments, various types of bucket fittings, knives and fire-steels. The finds of keys are interesting too. Hooked types are represented by finds from a private collection. Craft tools, or parts of them, are so far known (apart from the axes) only from the hillfort. They are represented by saw blades, axes, a drill bit (fig. 10: 1, 2), shears, awls, ceramic loom weights and spindle whorls, and stone whetstones and smoothers. These objects attest the work of craftsmen such as woodworking, the manufacture of clothing and the production of pottery, indirectly attested by numerous finds of sherd material, which was wheel-thrown and provided above all with the typical bands of wavy lines and grooves. Smithing is attested by finds of tongs. Connected with it is also the production of semi-finished products that were at the same time currency – axe-shaped currency bars in various sizes, found both whole and often in fragments.
Jewellery

Evidence of the classic horizon of the Great Moravian period is provided by finds of women's jewellery of the Danubian type, represented by five bronze earrings (one gilded) found on the first bailey, reportedly at the point of the section through the rampart. Also fitting into this horizon is the find of a gilded
gombík

and a hoard consisting of seven earrings (two in Byzantine-Oriental style, one of them gilded, the other silvered), a bronze gombík and a finger ring from a hut found on the acropolis, together with a whole vessel, a spearhead and a dagger. It appears that the dwelling was destroyed by fire. In view of the contents of the hoard we may consider the demise of the feature sometime from the end of the 9th to the course of the first half of the 10th century. Among the other Slavic jewellery we may mention a disc-shaped glass bead, a glass gombík and a bronze ring bezel decorated with repoussé work. The most recent finds include that of a gombík decorated with high-quality filigree work, typical of the Great Moravian period.
Dwellings and farm buildings

Today we know that the inhabitants built their dwellings on artificially levelled terraces as well as on natural platforms. We have a reasonably good idea of the inhabitants' dwellings, which were log buildings. As for the number of dwellings, it is difficult to establish. There may have been dozens of log buildings, providing shelter, at the height of the site's development, to several hundred inhabitants.

The hillfort also contained several non-residential, mostly smaller features of a farm character. These may have been sheds, pigsties or stables. Pits served as cool stores for food. The presence of production features is evident. It is indirectly attested by the finds of smith's tongs and slag mentioned above.
The construction of the defensive wall

children.text: The construction of the defensive wall on the acropolis consisted of earth with stones, reinforced by timber beams laid one above another – perhaps grillages. On the bailey side a stone wall was identified (the wall at least 4.5 m wide). On the outer side a ditch of conical shape was dug (2.6 m wide and 1.5 m deep). The inner ditch was not investigated here. This oldest fortified enclosure was about 325 m long and at least 170 m wide. The fortification of the first bailey was destroyed by fire. When this happened is hard to say. Even after it was abandoned the hillfort served as a refuge throughout the rest of the Middle Ages. The rampart of the first bailey was rebuilt twice; it was built of earth fixed with posts and beams and provided on the outer side with a stone wall (originally 3 m, after rebuilding 4.5–5 m). The effectiveness of the defences was increased by the doubling of the wall of the first bailey. The rampart of the second bailey, as well as the rebuilding of the first, evidently took place in the course of the second half of the 9th or at the beginning of the 10th century. Ditches dug in front of the ramparts were also part of the defences. The total length of the fortified area after the bailey defences were added reached approximately 680 m, including the low rampart of the second bailey, which has not been investigated so far. The entrance gateways into the hillfort may likewise be expected on the longitudinal axis.
Further occupation of the hillfort after the fall of Great Moravia

The representation of finds at the hillfort is temporarily interrupted at the end of the 10th century. For the next 200 years or so it was again only a temporary refuge in times of attack. This state of affairs changed only with the arrival of the counts of Svätý Jur and Pezinok, under whose ownership permanent occupation was renewed for the period from the beginning of the 13th to the end of the 14th century. It was they who had a palace building, a water cistern and a clay pipeline about 3 kilometres long built. At the same time they also renewed the rampart system and added to it a gateway corresponding to the trends of the time in the building of noble residences.
The archaeologist Július Vavák presents the hillfort and the most interesting finds from it:

Although the counts saw to the rebuilding of the hillfort, only a few decades later they set about building a stone castle on the hill on the other side of the valley. This probably happened after the Mongol invasion of 1241. After they moved to Biely Kameň castle, a permanent garrison was maintained at the original hillfort for a considerable time. Only very few finds were recovered in the ruins of the medieval residential buildings, which testifies to a peaceful departure of the inhabitants from the hillfort. After the hillfort was abandoned in the course of the 14th century, there was never again permanent occupation on its territory, although it is possible that the inhabitants of the surrounding settlements used the existing rampart system as a refuge in some of the fighting of the following decades.
The medieval water pipeline

At the time of the medieval occupation it was necessary to ensure a constant supply of drinking water to the area of the hillfort. This was served by a clay pipeline built over a length of several kilometres, which created a link between the hillfort and a spring outside the rampart system. The pipeline was made of clay. Its individual sections measured 55–58 cm and, with internal diameters of 8.5–13.0 and 7.7–13.0, the individual sections fitted perfectly one into another. Besides the pipes it also included small shafts, which served to vent it and also to trap dirt and sludge. Individual sections of the pipeline have been coming to light for several decades during various excavation works. Some of the discoveries ended up in the town museum, but also in the private collections of the finders.
Access to the hillfort and its signposting:
Neštich is one of those Slavic hillforts with a relatively
easy approach and clear, well-arranged signposting.

You drive through the centre of Jur, straight on at the roundabout, past the well-known medieval church with its wonderful acoustics (some notable high-quality CDs were recorded here – for example Godár's Mater project), then the road forks; by car it is easier to go right, and after about 150 metres there is a car park. The asphalt road continues beyond it, with a no-entry sign. Fit walkers need not hesitate and can set off straight up the steep slope across the contours, arriving directly at the hillfort; those who prefer comfort will follow the asphalt road, which forks after a few hundred metres. Here you turn left, and at the top of the hill left again, and you are at the hillfort. In front of the outer rampart stands a large stone with the carved inscription „Veľkomoravské hradisko“ (Great Moravian hillfort), and beside it we find a very nicely produced
information panel
on the history of the hillfort.
I commend this and I am glad that hillforts signposted like this are also to be found in Slovakia.
